This inner work is invisible, but it is what lets you rebuild your life rather than just deal with the consequences.

The difficulty is the silence. The decision ripened long ago, but those close to you only learn about it when everything is already happening. For you it is a closed chapter; for them it is a bolt from the blue. Their confusion seems strange to you, since you said your goodbyes long ago. Besides, a premonition is not always right: you can bury in advance something that was still alive and later discover that the collapse happened largely because you yourself stopped holding it up.

16-13-11.heading: Closing chapters with your composure intact
paragraphs: Your changes are never cosmetic. The Tower shows in your affairs: if the way your life is set up no longer matches reality, you don’t touch up the facade — you take the whole structure down. Death explains where your energy comes from: from endings — when a worn-out form goes, room and strength are freed for a new one. And Strength governs your feelings: even at the sharpest turn you keep your composure and meet a loss with courage, without panic.

**You have the courage to admit that a chapter is over and to begin the next one on a clean site.** Say a business you have run for years no longer brings either joy or income. Others would hang on to it out of habit, while you close it down, give away the equipment and say goodbye to your clients. It is sad, but calm. And six months later something is already growing in the freed-up space — something you simply never had the energy for before.

The flip side is a habit of ending things before they have had a chance to come right. If something gets difficult, your hand reaches for the switch of its own accord: it is easier to knock it down and start again than to repair it. And composure gets in the way of living through a loss: you hold yourself so steady that grieving seems to have neither time nor reason. Unmourned losses pile up, and one day yet another ending feels heavier than it should — not because of itself, but because of all the earlier ones you so bravely failed to notice.

16-14-3.heading: Growing something new where things broke
paragraphs: After a storm, some people first count the damage, while others go to see what survived and what can be planted again. In your field the second habit is stronger. The Tower brings storms to your affairs — sudden breakdowns after which the old arrangement cannot be restored. Temperance distributes your strength: you spend it in portions, mixing work, rest and care into a proportion that lasts. And the Empress in your feelings brings joy in everything that grows and lives in your care.

**Where something has broken, you begin not with building but with care.** Say a business you lived for has closed. You do not rush to put up something new at once. First you set the simple things right: home life, conversations with those close to you, a small activity that gives you pleasure. Out of this soil a new venture gradually grows — and it holds, because it grew from real interest rather than from panic.

The weak spot is going on tending something that can no longer grow. You have a lot of care to give, and it readily flows into a project that collapses again and again, or into a relationship the other side stopped needing long ago. Temperance suggests a little more patience, the Empress a little more warmth. But some breakdowns cannot be mended by tending: the foundation simply does not hold. Strength put into such soil does not come back, and admitting that is also a way of caring for yourself.

16-14-12.heading: No hurry to rebuild what has fallen
paragraphs: Sometimes what you built with great effort — a plan, a way of life, a shared venture — falls apart faster than you can understand why. That is what the Tower says in the overall rhythm of what you do: whatever stood on shaky ground stops holding one day, and the loss can be real. Your strength, though, comes not from a sudden push but from Temperance — from the knack of combining different things little by little: old experience with new conditions, what you want with what others are able to give. And the Hanged Man sets your response: at a hard moment you do not rush about; your feelings seem to freeze, and for a while you see the world from an unfamiliar angle.

**After a collapse, what you need is not speed but time to see what everything rested on.** While others hurry to put everything back as it was, you stop and look at what happened differently: what was a real support, and what only seemed to be one. Then the quiet work begins — some of the old you can take with you, and some you will have to leave behind. The new takes shape slowly, but it has a chance not to stand on the same crack.

The difficulty is that the pause can drag on. Your feelings stay suspended, the decision keeps being put off, and Temperance keeps blending and reconciling: you are sorry to lose the old, and the new frightens you. In the end the pieces are carefully glued back onto the old foundation — it feels gentler and more familiar that way. From the outside your life has been put back together, but that very crack has not gone anywhere, and the next jolt lands in the same place.

16-15-4.heading: A fortress held up by a tight grip
paragraphs: You feel calmer when everything is within reach and arranged by clear rules. That is the voice of the Emperor in your overall emotional tone: order is how you feel the ground under your feet. What drives you, though, is the Devil — a strong pull towards what you want to have and keep: a position, possessions, people, a familiar way of life. It is this grip that gives you persistence. But next to it, in what you do, stands the Tower: what you build collapses from time to time, and collapses sharply, if it rested more on the wish to hold on than on solid foundations.

**You can rebuild, as long as you see honestly what held the old structure up.** When the familiar falls apart, you do not lose your head: you take charge, hand out tasks and bring order to what is left. The pull that used to tie you to the old can become strength for the new — if you admit it plainly: “I want this, and this is what I pay for it.” Then the new order rests on more than grip alone.

It gets harder when your answer to every collapse is an even tighter grip. Higher walls, stricter rules, closer control — anything to stop it happening again. But what is held up by the sheer effort of holding on does not become sturdier; it only becomes more strained. When a loss does come, it feels like losing control of your own life, and the circle starts again: the same pull, the same walls, the same risk.

16-15-13.heading: Letting go of what has already fallen
paragraphs: What do you do with something that has already collapsed but still holds you? Your attachments are strong — that is the Devil — and a great deal of your strength goes into what you hold dear. So when the Tower cuts something off in your affairs all at once — an agreement, a job, a familiar way of life — you feel the loss with your whole being. Death in your emotional response gives you the ability to live through this ending in earnest: not to pretend nothing has happened, but to grieve and admit that the old form is gone.

**You can admit that the old is gone, and that is exactly what gives you back your choice.** Say a project you put several years into has been shut down. At first it is hard: you want to call people, find out what happened, look for a way to bring it all back. But a moment comes when you honestly tell yourself: “It’s over.” Grief is still grief, but the pull stops making decisions for you, and your strength returns to what is still alive.

The danger zone lies between the break and the goodbye. The pull keeps you inside something that has already cracked: you feel that its form is spent, but attachment will not let you be the first to leave. Then the end comes not as a quiet close but as a collapse, and the loss turns out bigger than it had to be. And after the collapse the pull easily moves on to the wreckage — rereading, going back, proving your point — and the goodbye is put off once again.

16-16-5.heading: Values that can stand the truth
paragraphs: Accepted rules, family customs, shared values — you need something like this to lean on. The Hierophant in your emotional tone makes belonging a source of calm: it feels good when it is clear what the right way is. But the Tower stands in two places at once, and its roles are different. In what you do, it brings breaking points: something that looked unshakeable can collapse once its weakness comes to light. In how your strength is spread, it works differently — tension builds up while the appearance of order holds, and comes out in a burst when pretending is no longer possible.

**It matters to you that the order you trust can stand up to the truth.** When a rule turns out to be empty and an authority hollow, you do not lose your footing completely: you can tell a living value from its frozen form. For example, a custom kept for many years falls apart, and you hold on to what it was for — care, getting together, mutual support — rather than the ceremony itself.

It becomes hard if you defend the form for longer than it can hold. The people around you expect everything to be done as it always has been, and you keep the facade up even though the cracks are already showing. Your strength goes into keeping up appearances, and it gets released anyway — only later and more violently. Then the collapse hits twice: you lose the thing itself, and your belief that there is such a thing as a right way at all.

16-16-14.heading: A steady heart in an uneven life
paragraphs: The outward course of your life is seldom smooth. The Tower in what you do means sharp turns: plans break off, and arrangements that seemed solid suddenly stop working. In how your strength is spread, the same card sounds different — energy comes not as an even flow but in surges: it builds up for a long time and is released all at once. And inside there is Temperance. You can blend fright and sober calculation, the bitterness of loss and whatever has survived, into one.

**You can live through a sharp turn without losing the ability to join one thing with another.** Say a venture you were counting on suddenly closes. It hurts, and you do not hide it, but you do not slide into panic either: you look for what from the old will still be useful, who you can bring in, how to get through to the next stage. Around you, others calm down too — your sense of measure helps them find their own.

But your knack for smoothing everything over can end up fooling you. You dilute every worry and explain away every crack, and for a long time it feels inside as if all is well. Signals that could have warned you in advance never reach your feelings, while the tension keeps building. Then it comes out in a surge again, and once again it seems that life has struck out of nowhere, although this time the signs were there to see.

16-18-7.heading: Pressing ahead on a misty road
paragraphs: When something collapses, your first feeling is not confusion but the urge to break through. The Chariot in your emotional response pulls you together: take the reins, choose a direction, prove that there is a road after all. The strength for this often comes from the Moon — from imagination, hunches, pictures of a possible future that carry you away more than facts do. And the Tower in what you do is a reminder of the price: a plan built on a guess can one day collapse entirely.

**You can move forward when not everything is visible, as long as you can tell the road from its reflection.** Your imagination suggests moves that others do not notice, and the Chariot’s determination keeps you from freezing in doubt. Say a plan falls apart at the last moment. You do not give up: you check which of your earlier assumptions turned out to be false, and build the next move on what is known for certain.

The difficulty begins when the reflection is taken for the road. A beautiful picture ahead beckons, excitement spurs you on, and checking the foundations seems like a waste of time. The plan rests on a guess, and when it collapses, the Chariot at once demands a new dash forward, while the Moon is already painting a new picture. In this way you can build on fog several times in a row and each time take the collapse for a piece of bad luck.

16-18-16.heading: Lightning that tears through the fog
paragraphs: There is a lot of half-light in the overall tone of your life. The Moon makes your strength depend on what is unclear: you are guided by hunches, guesses and imagination, and worry about the unknown can take more energy than the task itself. The Tower appears twice, in two different roles. In what you do, it means that whatever is flimsy collapses one day — an agreement, a plan, a familiar order. In your emotions, it is the moment when the truth is revealed all at once: a moment ago the picture seemed whole, and suddenly you can see what it was resting on.

**Your strength lies in not looking away when appearances fall apart.** Many people live for years in a comfortable haze. For you, insight comes like a lightning strike, and after it it is hard to pretend nothing has happened. It hurts, and the loss is real. But you stop investing in what rested on an illusion, and the fog lifts, at least in that one place.

The danger is that in the half-light it is easy to imagine a collapse before it happens. A vague signal, a delayed reply, a change in someone’s tone — and your imagination has already filled in the wreck. Inside, everything falls apart as if the truth had been revealed, although it was only a shadow. If you act on that feeling, you can break with your own hands something that was actually standing firm.

17-1-9.heading: Giving outwardly, reflecting within
paragraphs: From the outside, you are someone who shares readily. The Star sets the overall rhythm of what you do: you act openly, with no hidden agenda, and what you make often benefits more than just you — a tip, a helping hand, something finished, time spent on someone. The Magician gives you the strength for this: you are charged by your own skill, by the chance to take whatever is at hand and turn an intention into a result. Your feelings, however, go their own way. The Hermit in your emotional response takes you into silence: you first need to understand what you have been through on your own.

**You give away what you make generously, but you make sense of what happens by yourself.** Say a friend is in trouble. You come over, fix things, negotiate, find the right person — your hands and head work fast. But afterwards you need an evening alone to work out what you yourself feel about it all. From that solitude you often bring back a clear thought, which you then share as well.

The difficulty lies in the gap between what others see and what goes on inside. People get used to your open help and do not know that things are sometimes hard for you too: you say nothing about your feelings until you have sorted them out. When your strength runs low, you simply withdraw into yourself without explaining anything. The people close to you take it for coldness, you take it for an ordinary breather, and misunderstanding grows on both sides.

17-4-12.heading: Giving in good order, feeling it later
paragraphs: Your feelings often arrive not at the moment of the event but later, when everything has already been done. That is the Hanged Man in your overall emotional response: the experience seems to hang in the air, and you see what happened from the side, differently than in the heat of the moment. While your feelings wait, your hands work. The Star makes what you do open and generous: you help without calculation and do not hide what you can do. The Emperor gives you the strength for it — giving is easier when it is clear how everything is arranged, what you are responsible for and where your part ends.

**It is easier for you to be generous when your generosity has a structure.** Suppose a crisis hits your family or your workplace. You sort out who does what, take on a clear area of your own and give it everything you can. Your feeling about what is happening ripens later and often brings an unexpected view: it becomes clear what really mattered, and next time you arrange things differently.

The trouble is that the pause can become a way of life. Order has been restored, help has been given, and your own feelings stay on the “later” pile. The Emperor keeps everything under control, the Star goes on giving, and there is never a moment to ask yourself: and how am I doing? Months go by, the experience hangs there unsorted, and one day tiredness arrives before you understand where it came from.

17-5-13.heading: Passing it on and letting go
paragraphs: Much of what you do resembles passing something on: knowledge, a craft, care — you give them to others openly, without trying to keep them for yourself. This is how the Star shows in the overall rhythm of what you do. You draw the strength for it from the Hierophant — from belonging to something larger: a tradition, a community, a circle of people with shared values, people you once learned from yourself. And Death in your emotional response makes you sensitive to endings: you can clearly feel when a stage is over, and you know how to live through it.

**You can give away what you were given and let go of what has already been passed on.** For example, you taught someone your craft, and they went their own way. You feel sad, but you do not hold on to them through gratitude or a sense of debt: what you passed on now lives on without you. You live through each such farewell in earnest, and that is why it leaves you with a sense of completion rather than resentment.

Difficulty arises when your source of strength and your sense of an ending pull apart. The community has changed, the familiar circle has broken up, the rules have lost their old meaning — inside, you already know this stage is over. But your strength still comes from belonging, and you keep giving out of duty: turning up, helping, keeping up the form. Generosity turns into a ritual with no life left in it, while a new place for it never quite appears.

17-6-14.heading: Generosity that would rather not choose
paragraphs: You have enough strength as long as there is someone to share it with: the Lovers make your bonds with the people you chose with your heart a source of energy — a partner, friends, the people you work with. For their sake the generosity of the Star becomes an everyday thing: you openly give your time, attention and skills and do not keep count. When friction arises between the people close to you, Temperance steps in. You do not take sides in the heat of the moment but look for a way to join two wishes, so that neither has to be destroyed.

**Around you, it is easier for people to stay together.** Say an argument is brewing in your family about where to spend the holidays. You do not push and do not step aside: you listen to both sides, suggest an option where each gets something, and take on part of the fuss yourself. The holiday turns out to belong to everyone, and that gives you more strength than the preparations took.

It is harder when a situation calls for a choice, not a middle ground. The Lovers sometimes put the question bluntly: whose side are you on, what matters more to you? Temperance looks for an option where nobody loses, and the Star keeps giving a little to everyone. The decision is put off, you spread yourself across everyone, and each person gets slightly less than they expected — while the one who matters most never gets to hear that they do.

17-7-6.heading: A goal you want to share
paragraphs: Your goals are rarely yours alone. The Chariot gives you strength: you are charged by direction, by an obstacle overcome, by the sense that the work is moving. The Star in the overall rhythm of what you do adds hope and openness to that movement — you take things on in a way that makes it brighter around you, and you readily share your plan, your energy and your belief that it will work. And the Lovers decide how you experience the result: success truly delights you when there is someone to share it with.

**A goal warms you more when you do not head towards it alone.** Say you have started a renovation, a move or a joint project. You see before others how it could all look, you get everyone else excited about it, and you pull the work along when someone gets tired. But the real celebration comes when someone close to you says: “We did it.” The victory becomes shared, and the strength for the next step comes from it.

The difficulty is that the movement can outrun the people it was started for. The Chariot is already racing, the Star generously promises that good things lie ahead, and it seems that the person beside you wants the same. Their doubts look like a delay, their slower pace like a hindrance. You pull them along with the best of intentions, while they feel that nobody asked them. The goal is reached, but you can no longer enjoy it together.

17-7-15.heading: Giving everything, holding on to the outcome
paragraphs: Putting in half an effort is not your way. The Star sets the overall rhythm of what you do: you give openly and generously — time, energy, ideas — without working out in advance what you will get back. The Chariot adds direction: your strength grows when there is a goal and the work is visibly moving towards it. And in your emotions stands the Devil, and here everything is serious. You become firmly attached to whatever you have invested in: the outcome moves you deeply, and letting go of it is not easy.

**You invest in earnest, and it shows in how strongly the outcome affects you.** The people around you can feel that the work is no formality for you: you burn with it, drive it forward, rejoice at every step. If you admit this attachment honestly — “yes, it matters to me that this works out” — it becomes fuel rather than a chain. Then you can put everything in and still keep the freedom to choose when to stop.

The trap appears when the generosity outside and the attachment inside start to drift apart. Outwardly you give freely, but inside you are already clinging to the result: that the person stays, the project takes off, your efforts get noticed. If the outcome is not the one you wanted, the Chariot pushes you to press harder, and the Devil will not let you back down. A gift quietly turns into an investment that expects a return, and disappointment arrives before you have had time to notice.

17-8-7.heading: Generosity with measure and direction
paragraphs: In what you do, you resemble the figure on the Star who pours water from two vessels — onto the land and into the pool. You readily give your time, your skills, your help, and work goes best when it brightens things not only for you. Justice keeps an eye on how your strength is shared out: evenly between the work, the people close to you and yourself, with nothing lopsided. And the Chariot colours your feelings: what pleases you is the sense that everything is moving towards a goal and every step brings it nearer.

**Your generosity doesn’t spill everywhere because it has a measure and a direction.** Say you have offered to help some friends start a small business: you share your experience, your contacts, your evenings. But from the outset you agree how much time you are ready to give and what should be in place by when. Help becomes not an endless rescue mission but a shared road with clear stages — and every stage completed pleases you as much as it pleases them.

The difficulty comes when what you give doesn’t turn into movement. You shared generously and fairly, yet the business stands still: others don’t do their part, deadlines slide, your contribution comes back neither as results nor as thanks. The Chariot hates standing still, and inside you a tally begins: how much has gone in, how much has come back. Generosity that used to flow freely starts being handed out against receipts. Helping gets harder — not because you begrudge it, but because the sense of a road has gone.

17-8-16.heading: Openness that won’t forgive pretence
paragraphs: Life is easier for you when there is nothing to hide. The Star sets your way of acting: you share your plans, help without conditions and hope for the best — in people and in things. Justice governs your strength: it is fed by fair exchange, when what you give and what you receive are roughly in balance. And your feelings come by way of the Tower: emotionally, the strongest moment is when a false foundation is suddenly exposed and gives way.

**You build relationships on trust and are ready to see the truth, even if it shatters the picture.** Say you spent years helping a friend and believed the friendship was equal. Then one chance conversation reveals that you are being talked about behind your back. It is a blow, but you don’t hide from it: you admit you were wrong, draw your conclusions and keep the ability to trust — though no longer blindly. The collapse clears space for relationships where what you give comes back.

The danger lies between generosity and suddenness. You give openly and for a long time fail to notice an imbalance: hope explains away any inequality as a temporary difficulty. The account builds up in silence — and then everything collapses at once. For the other person this can come as a complete surprise: yesterday you were there for them, today it is “we’re finished”. After a collapse like that it is hard to open up again, and the next person gets less light than they might have — paying for someone else’s debts.

17-9-8.heading: Shining for others, refuelling in silence
paragraphs: Sharing comes naturally to you. The Star shows in the way you act: time, advice and skills are given generously, as if water were pouring from a jug, and that is the kind of work you do best. But the water in that jug is refilled in silence. The Hermit explains where your strength comes from: from hours alone, a road of your own, an inner lantern by whose light you work out what is what. And Justice governs your feelings: you are at peace when the exchange is fair and everyone receives according to their deeds.

**You shine for others precisely because you keep coming back to your own light.** For example, all day you explain, help and answer colleagues’ questions. And in the evening you need quiet — a walk without headphones, a book, no conversations. By morning you are ready to give again, and you give generously, but without strain. The people close to you who understand this rhythm receive warm, clear-headed attention from you.

Things get hard when solitude is taken for coldness and generosity for a duty. You have given a lot, but no one has left you any quiet: the evening is again taken up with other people’s requests, and saying no feels unfair to those who are waiting. Inside grows a sense of an unfair exchange: you shine, but you aren’t allowed to refuel. Resentment builds up in silence, and one day you withdraw into yourself for a long time — not to rest, but to wall yourself off. Then the people close to you lose both your generosity and your warmth at once.

17-9-17.heading: A guiding light without a crowd
paragraphs: In your overall tone the Star sounds twice, and it means two different things. In what you do, it is generosity: you give away what you know and can do, openly and without conditions. In your emotions, it is an inner guiding star: even after a hard stage, hope comes back, and what you have been through does not put out your belief that there is something worth trying for ahead. Between them stands the Hermit. You draw strength from your own path — from reflection, from solitude, from experience you reached by yourself.

**You can be a light for others without becoming anyone’s everyday guide.** Say someone close to you is going through a hard time. You do not take their life into your own hands or bury them in advice. You tell them how you went through something similar yourself — honestly, without embellishment — and that is often enough for hope to appear in them too. The light is passed on as an example, not as supervision.

The other side is hope kept in solitude. The inner guiding star climbs very high, and real people and real situations fall short of it. Every disappointment takes you into yourself, to the place where the ideal stays untouched. You gladly support others, but you keep quiet about your own loss and wait for the light to return on its own. It may return, but by then fewer and fewer people around you know that things were dark for you.

17-10-9.heading: Knowing where you are on the wheel
paragraphs: Highs and lulls follow one another, and your energy moves with them. The Wheel of Fortune means that your energy depends on the turns of life: there are periods when everything falls into place and you want to take on a lot, and periods when circumstances change against your will. On the rise, the Star shines brightly — you spend yourself generously on work and people, share readily and make promises. And your emotional response belongs to the Hermit: you need to understand every turn, and for that you step aside and look at what has happened in silence.

**You give more generously when you understand where you are on the wheel.** A downturn does not frighten you as a failure: you see it as part of the movement, use the pause to make sense of the last stage and come out of it with a clear conclusion. When the wheel turns again, you already know what is worth spending your energy on and what is better not to start.

The difficulty is that the wheel does not wait until you have thought everything through. On the rise, the Star hands out promises, counting on your energy lasting. Then the wheel turns, your energy drops, and you withdraw to sort things out. People who were counting on you see only that you have disappeared. Understanding comes, but later than you needed to give an answer, and the promises are left hanging.

17-10-18.heading: Hope in shifting light
paragraphs: Things left unsaid, a shift in people’s mood, a vague premonition — you pick these up before anyone has named them. The Moon in your emotional response gives you this sensitivity, but its light is reflected, and in it fear or fantasy is easily mistaken for knowledge. Your energy comes in waves, following the Wheel of Fortune: circumstances change, and your energy now rises, now ebbs away. Your footing in this changeable world is the Star in what you do: open, clear actions in which you give rather than hide.

**What helps you is doing something clear while your feelings are still unsettled.** Say an uncertain period begins: a change of job, a move, changes in the family. Inside, things sway, and your imagination paints first one picture, then another. And you keep doing simple things — helping, finishing what you started, supporting the people close to you. Your hope rests not on guessing the future but on the fact that every day you give something.

It gets harder when every turn of the wheel starts to read as a sign. A quiet week becomes “everything is going downhill”, a delayed reply becomes a bad omen. Imagination fills the gaps, anxiety grows, and the Star’s generosity gives way to wariness: you hold back your energy, do not start things, wait for confirmation. Meanwhile circumstances change again, but you are already acting on the picture the Moon painted, not on what is actually happening.

17-11-1.heading: Inspiring and getting straight to work
paragraphs: There is a lot of light in your overall tone. The Star shows in your affairs: you act openly and generously, and you gladly put yourself into whatever brings benefit and hope to others. Strength governs your energy: it comes from calm composure — the ability to deal gently with your own fears and outbursts without wasting yourself on a fight. And in your feelings the Magician leads: the brightest feeling comes when an idea turns into a result thanks to your own hands and mind.

**You don’t just cheer people on — you show that hope can be made real.** Say your neighbours have long dreamed of a playground in the courtyard. While everyone else sighs, you calmly collect signatures, find a contractor, sort it out with the housing association. A couple of months later children are already on the swings, and you feel that special joy of something coming together because you found a way to do it.

The vulnerable spot is other people’s troubles that you can’t solve. Generosity pulls you to help, composure lets you keep going for a long time, and satisfaction comes only when you have influenced the outcome. But when the outcome doesn’t depend on you — someone else’s heavy loss, a decision a person has to make alone — confusion rises inside: you are there, but there is nothing to do. And then you take on anything at all just to be acting, though sometimes a person simply needs you to be there.

17-11-10.heading: Waiting out the bottom of the wheel
captions: Back to work after a slump
paragraphs: You tend to believe that a rise will follow a fall. The Star sets the rhythm of your affairs: you act with open hope, return to work quickly after a hard stretch and gladly share what you have. Strength explains where your energy comes from: from a gentle self-possession that doesn’t let panic take over. And the Wheel of Fortune sounds in your feelings: your mood clearly follows the course of events — success gives you wings, failure bows you down, and you know this about yourself.

**You know how to wait out the bottom of the wheel without losing your light.** Say a year turns out to be hard: the orders dry up, plans fall through. You admit that this is a low point and don’t pretend to be cheerful — but you don’t sink into despair either. You do the little that can be done and support those who have it even harder. And when the wheel turns, you are the first to be ready, because all that time you never put out your hope.

The flip side is a habit of waiting for the turn instead of looking for it. If you always believe that “it’ll pass soon”, you can stand still for too long: patiently, calmly, hopefully. The wheel really does turn, but not necessarily in the direction you need. And when the rise is slow to come, calm gives way to weariness, and hope to a quiet grudge against fate — although fate never promised anything.

17-12-2.heading: Gifts that ripen in silence
paragraphs: From the outside it is plain how much you give: you share what you have found, support people, bring a finished result to the common cause. That is the Star — an open, generous way of acting. What cannot be seen is where all of it comes from. The Hanged Man suggests that your strength arrives in stillness, when you can stop striving for anything and look at life from a different angle. The High Priestess takes your feelings inward: you feel a great deal, and deeply, and are in no hurry to put it into words.

**The best of what you give others first ripens in silence.** Say someone close to you faces a difficult choice. You do not shower them with advice: you listen, take a pause, carry the question around inside you for a few days. Then you come back with a thought that genuinely helps, because you have had time to see the situation from an unfamiliar side. People feel at ease around you: you rush neither them nor yourself.

The difficulty is that quiet work stays invisible. When someone asks “what’s wrong?”, you answer “I’m fine”, while inside a big change is already under way. The people close to you see only the pause and wonder what it means. Then you come out with a decision already made, and they feel hurt: everything was thought through without them. You share the result generously but let hardly anyone in on the road to it — and so you get no support along the way either.

17-12-11.heading: Giving generously and knowing when to stop
captions: A new view after a pause
paragraphs: Sometimes the best way to help is to stop for a while. The Star shows in your affairs: time, hands and attention are given generously, without long calculation, and work goes best when someone needs it. The Hanged Man explains how your strength works: it comes back during a pause, when you step out of the bustle and look at everything from a different angle. And your feelings pass through Strength: you meet strong emotions, your own and other people’s, calmly and with quiet courage.

**Your generosity doesn’t run dry because you know how to stop in time and look at things differently.** Say for several months you have been helping a friend through a difficult divorce: talks, a house move, paperwork. At some point you are running on empty — and instead of playing the hero, you take a couple of days’ break. You come back with a fresh view: what he needs now is not looking after but faith that he will manage on his own. And that change helps you both.

The risk is a pause that becomes a way of life. Putting your own plans aside for someone else comes so naturally that whole years get put aside: a trip, a course of study, a business of your own — “when it’s possible”. Calm composure helps you not notice the cost: you don’t complain, you don’t snap, you keep everything in hand. But light that is given without return eventually dims. And it turns out that you are hanging upside down not for the sake of a new view, but simply out of habit.

17-13-12.heading: Between an ending and a new start
paragraphs: Your life moves not in a straight line but in stages. Death shows where your strength comes from: you come alive once what has had its day is closed — a job, a way of life, a way of spending your time. The Hanged Man shapes how you live through it: between an ending and a beginning you seem to hang in mid-air, see the familiar upside down and are in no hurry to draw conclusions. The Star leads you out of this pause into action: once a new meaning is found, you take on the work with hope and put yourself into it generously.

**For you the pause between stages is not empty — a new view takes shape in it.** Say a big project has come to an end. Someone else would grab the next one straight away, but you spend a few weeks without hurrying, sorting out what really mattered and what was kept up out of habit. Then a clear “this is what I want” appears — and you start not from scratch but with a hope you can name.

The suspended state can drag on. The old is closed, the new has no name yet, and it seems that any moment now everything will become clear. While your own beginning keeps being put off, your hands are busy with other people’s: you generously help others launch their ventures, support them, give advice. From the outside it looks like a busy life, yet your own new page stays blank. The longer this goes on, the more daunting it is to begin.

17-14-4.heading: Giving in measure, keeping order
paragraphs: A friend’s request, a work project, household chores, someone’s new venture that needs support — you manage to take part in a great deal. The Star in your actions is not stingy: you put yourself in wherever you can be useful. Temperance shares out your strength: a little here, a little there, alternating effort with rest so there is enough for everything. And the Emperor is in charge of your inner calm: you feel good when life has structure — a plan, clear rules, clarity about who is responsible for what.

**Your generosity rests on a well-thought-out order.** You know which day to help your parents, when to see to your own affairs, how much time to give to someone else’s request. That is exactly why you can promise a lot and deliver: your strength is shared out in advance. You experience success as proof that the system works, and you meet uncertainty in your usual way — you draw up a plan and immediately feel solid ground underfoot.

The weak spot is whatever does not fit the schedule. Someone close comes to you with a sudden misfortune, or work demands that everything be rearranged at once. You are ready to help, but irritation arrives before the wish to help: the order your calm rests on is collapsing. You do help, but drily and point by point, and the person feels they have become a nuisance. Generosity that switches on only according to plan starts to look like an obligation — both to you and to those you give it to.

17-14-13.heading: Letting go without bitterness
paragraphs: The hardest thing about change is the moment of farewell, and this is exactly where you have a strength of your own. Death in emotions means you take the end of a stage seriously: a parting, leaving a job, a relationship that has changed — none of it passes you by. Temperance spreads your strength smoothly: you blend the old with the new, shift your attention little by little and do not swing from one extreme to the other. The Star guides your actions: even in a time of loss you keep acting with hope and sharing what you have.

**You know how to say goodbye so that life still has a sequel.** Say a close friend is moving far away. You allow yourself to be sad, but you neither cut the tie nor cling to the old routine: you help them pack, agree on a new rhythm for keeping in touch, find something to fill the evenings that have opened up. Sadness and gratitude mix, and the change becomes part of your life rather than a hole in it.

There is a flip side: your inner farewell can run ahead of everyone else’s. You have already lived through the ending, accepted it and moved smoothly on, while the people around you are still in the thick of the parting. Your calm looks like coldness to them: “don’t you care at all?” Yet you gave it a great deal of feeling — just earlier and more quietly. If you do not tell them what you went through, all they will see is how easily you let go of what is dear to them.

17-15-5.heading: Generosity on the hook of approval
paragraphs: What makes you get up earlier and take on extra? Most often a strong desire: to be needed, for the result to happen, for what is dear to you to stay close. The Devil in energy speaks of exactly this kind of pull: it supplies plenty of fuel, but it also binds. The Star makes your actions open and generous: you put yourself in where everyone can see, you help, you share. The Hierophant adds an emotional yardstick: you feel at peace when what you have done fits accepted values and wins the approval of the circle you belong to.

In the family, at work, in a community, you are the one who takes on more than was asked, and does it wholeheartedly. **You burn brightest when your contribution serves a shared cause you respect.** Recognition from your own people brings deep satisfaction: you feel you are in the right place and doing the right thing. Here desire and values pull in the same direction.

The trap closes when approval itself becomes the hook. You want to give no longer because you have something to give, but because without praise you feel uneasy. You agree to yet another request although you have no strength left — that is how it is done, that is what people expect of you. Your own wish hides behind “I have to”, and saying no feels like betraying your circle. The generosity remains, but the freedom to choose whom to give to, and how much, slowly fades away.

17-15-14.heading: Strong attraction and an even heart
paragraphs: There are pursuits and people you find hard to tear yourself away from. The Devil explains where your strength comes from on the whole: from strong attraction — to a task, a pleasure, a person, a result. The Star directs this force outward: you do not hoard it but invest it generously in what you love. Temperance sets the emotional tone: even strong feelings you mix, dilute and bring to measure, so on the outside you look calmer than the fire burning inside.

**You can get seriously carried away without losing your head.** An idea that grips you gives so much strength that work on it spills into evenings and weekends. But the joy of success does not intoxicate you, and failure does not knock you off your feet: your feelings find the middle ground. People feel safe with you — your passion for the work never turns into a storm that hits everyone around.

But evenness of feeling can mask attachment. Since everything inside is under control, the choice seems free too: “I can stop whenever I want.” Meanwhile more and more evenings go where the pull takes you, and everything else is put off. There is no alarm: your emotions are smoothed out, and it is hard to notice that the passion is already deciding by itself where your time goes. Usually this comes to light only when you really do need to stop.

17-16-6.heading: Rebuilding and choosing with the heart
paragraphs: Sometimes the familiar order collapses within a week: a plan proves impossible, an agreement turns out to be empty, your idea of yourself proves wrong. The Tower in energy means that your strength often arrives at exactly such moments: when what was false falls, a lot of energy is released for what is real. The Lovers shape your response: you live through everything important via people and via the choice of who is dear to you. And the Star in your actions is the ability to rebuild: after the storm you set about watering the scorched earth again.

**For you a shock often becomes a moment of honest choice.** When something big collapses, it becomes clear who is truly there for you and who you want to go on building with. You do not hide from this clarity: you decide with your heart and start acting at once — helping, supporting, putting everyday life back together. In hard times people are drawn to you, because around you hope appears again.

The flip side is that calm times can seem too dull. If your strength wakes up with a breakthrough, an ordinary uneventful day starts to weigh on you, and your feelings seem to fade. Then you are tempted to stage a test: “let’s be honest, what is going on between us?” — at midnight, out of the blue. The person close to you does not understand what has happened and gets defensive. A relationship that was simply going along starts to shake, because you were missing the clarity that only crises used to bring.

17-16-15.heading: Freedom your feelings catch up with later
paragraphs: You can break with what has had its day in a single day. Letting go of it in your feelings takes far longer. The Tower in energy gives you strength for decisive change: once it is clear the foundation was false, you do not cling to the appearance of stability. The Star makes your actions direct and open: you tell it as it is and begin again. And the Devil in emotions keeps the link with the past: you grow firmly attached to people, habits and places, and the chain does not break along with the decision.

You leave a job that long ago became a cage, and you honestly explain why. The new life falls into place, you are open to it and full of hope. Yet your thoughts keep returning to the old: you go over it, compare, miss even what weighed you down. **It can be easier for you to break free in deed than in feeling.** That is how deep attachment works, and there is nothing to be ashamed of. Once acknowledged, it stops making your decisions for you.

The circle closes if the pull of the old wins time after time. Once again you agree to “just this once”, once again you end up where you left. Then the moment of insight comes again, and the break is even louder. Each cycle feels like liberation, although in fact it repeats the one before. Your strength goes on tearing down and coming back, and almost none is left for living the loss through to the end.

17-17-7.heading: Following the light of your own star
paragraphs: You have an inner landmark — a sense of what life could be if there were more meaning, beauty or truth in it. The Star holds two positions here, and its roles are different. In energy it is a source: strength flows in from whatever inspires you — a thought, a meeting, a place that leaves you wanting to keep going. In your actions it is generosity: you do not keep what you have found to yourself but pass it on to others. The Chariot is in charge of your response: joy comes when you feel yourself moving towards a goal.

**You are guided by a light, and every step towards it feels like a victory.** An idea has inspired you — and you are already telling others about it, looking for allies, taking the first steps. Each stage you complete lifts your mood, and you meet a setback by taking a firmer grip on the reins. Around you, people find it easier to believe that what was planned is possible: your hope shows in your actions, not only in your words.

Difficulty begins when the movement stops. The work gets stuck at some stage, and your feelings immediately say: “defeat.” You want to push harder, prove yourself, speed up. But in the race you lose what fed your strength — the joy of the landmark itself. You keep giving and straining forward, while the source is never refilled. The Star dims not because the goal is false, but because there is no time left to look at it.

18-8-8.heading: Clear terms on shifting ground
paragraphs: Uncertainty wears you out not in itself but when it is unclear who is responsible for what. Justice governs both your strength and your response, but in different ways. In energy it is a support: strength appears when the terms are named and obligations are shared out and honestly kept. In emotions it is an inner set of scales: you live through events by asking whether what happened was deserved and whether both sides acted fairly. And the fog comes from the Moon: you often have to act in shifting circumstances, short of information.

**Where everything is shaky, you lean on clear agreements.** A project with no clear plan, a family situation where nobody knows what to do — the first thing you ask is who does what and by when. Once that is said out loud, the fog thins. A fair decision brings you relief even if it does not work in your favour, and the people around you get a better idea of what they can count on.

In moonlight, however, the scales can end up weighing guesses. It seems to you that someone is breaking the agreement: they gave an evasive answer, did something other than what they promised. Imagination fills in the picture, the inner scales pass a verdict, and the conversation begins with an accusation. The other person gets defensive, and you take this as confirmation. Justice is easier to reach if you first find out what happened and only then decide whether it was fair.

18-8-17.heading: Finding your way through fog by a star
paragraphs: Your undertakings often begin in uncertainty. The Moon sets your material rhythm: you move by instinct, feeling your way, and you can’t always explain why you chose this particular road. Justice governs your strength: clarity brings it back — when facts can be separated from impressions, weighed up and honestly named for what they are. And in your feelings the Star shines: even in a murky period there is hope ahead, and after a hard stage comes a sense of inner renewal.

**You let yourself walk into the unknown, but you check your route against the facts — and you don’t lose hope.** Say you move to a city where you don’t know anyone. The first decisions — where to live, what to take on — are made almost blindly, by feel. But every week you honestly take stock: what has been confirmed, what turned out to be an illusion. Little by little the fog lifts, and every new landmark is as welcome as a star in a break in the clouds.

It gets harder when the scales have nothing to rest on and imagination is only too happy to fill in. In a murky situation — someone’s silence, unclear conditions at work — the Moon will draw in what is missing, and the need for clarity will push you to reach a verdict based on those guesses. Hope, meanwhile, tips the scales towards the better version: “they’re just busy”, “it’ll all work out”. The decision looks well weighed, but what lay on the scales were not facts but moonlit reflections. And when the fog clears, the disappointment hits harder than an honest “I don’t know yet” would have.

18-9-9.heading: Working it out alone, coming back clear
paragraphs: When a situation is tangled, you do not rush into the general bustle — first you withdraw into yourself. The Hermit has two roles in your field. As a source of strength he stands for solitude: your energy comes back when you can be alone with your thoughts. As your response he sets the order of your feelings: an event first has to be thought through, and only then talked about. And the tangle often comes from the Moon: you act by impression, in situations where much has to be guessed.

There is confusion at work, and everyone is arguing. You take an evening to lay out for yourself what is known for sure and what only seems so. **You find your clarity alone, and then you shine it for others.** The next day you come in with a calm, considered view, and it becomes easier for people to get their bearings. It is like the Hermit with his lantern on the summit: the understanding you have reached becomes a light for those still below.

In the silence, though, the Moon keeps working. Alone with yourself, impressions easily turn into conclusions and guesses into certainty, and there is no one to check them against. You come back with a finished understanding that is partly built on imagination. The people close to you are surprised: everything has been decided without them, and it is hard to object now — you have been thinking about it for so long. Solitude gives clarity when, afterwards, you are ready to test it in conversation.

18-10-10.heading: Living by your own tides
paragraphs: The Moon waxes and wanes, the wheel turns — and the overall rhythm of your life has plenty of both. The Moon makes the very course of your affairs changeable: there are periods of clarity, when you take on a lot, and periods of twilight, when you move carefully and by guesswork. The Wheel of Fortune in energy means that your strength comes in waves: a rise gives way to a fall, and this is not a breakdown but a cycle. In emotions the same card governs your response: you live through events as turns, where a fall is followed by a rise.

**Your strength lies not in constancy but in recognising your phase.** On the rise you can take on big things: start a project, tackle something difficult, meet new people. On the ebb it is better to finish things off, sort things out, wait. When you live with this rhythm rather than against it, a lot gets done almost without strain. Failure does not feel final, nor success eternal: everything is moving.

But it is easy to start using the turns to explain what actually depends on you. The Moon adds imagination: you see signs in coincidences, and in one bad day the start of a bad streak. A decision is put off until “the right moment”, which never quite arrives. The wheel really does turn, but you can wait for it to turn forever, while what was in your hands stays undone all along.

18-11-11.heading: Walking through the fog at a calm pace
paragraphs: Much in your life has to be done without seeing the whole road. This is what the Moon looks like in the overall rhythm of what you do: moving forward by reflected light, by impressions and guesses, step by step into the unknown. Strength appears twice here, and its roles are different. In energy it is courage: your strength comes from being ready to meet the unfamiliar rather than run from it. In emotions it is gentleness: you do not suppress anxiety and strong feelings but soothe them, the way the woman on the card tames the lion.

A new job, a move, a task nobody has taken on before — you begin even though much is unclear. Your fears speak up and your imagination paints the worst, but you neither argue with them nor obey them: you acknowledge them, breathe out and take the next step. **You can walk into the unknown without letting fear choose the road.** The people around you pick up on this calm.

What lets you down here is the habit of coping alone. Instead of asking directly what is going on, you reassure yourself again and again: “I’ll manage, it’s just nerves.” The fog does not lift, because nobody has supplied the missing information. Your strength goes into inner work that no one sees. Yet one question or one request for help would be enough to make the road brighter.

18-12-12.heading: Letting the fog clear
paragraphs: The answer to a difficult question rarely comes to you on demand. You do a lot by impression and intuition, without seeing the whole picture — this is how the Moon shows itself. The Hanged Man appears twice. In energy he gives strength through stopping: you get your strength back when you can leave everything undecided and let things hang for a while. In emotions he changes the angle of view: you turn over what you have been through from different sides for a long time before you understand what you really feel.

Say you have to choose between two offers. You put the question aside, live an ordinary life for a few days — and one morning you see everything differently: what seemed most important moves into the background. **Clarity comes to you when you stop trying to force it.** A decision made after such a pause usually stands the test of time, and around you others learn not to rush an answer either.

But waiting does not always end with daybreak. While you wait for clarity, the Moon fills the pause with guesses and fears, and the fog grows thicker, not thinner. People around you are waiting for an answer, deadlines pass, the offer is withdrawn. You say “I need to think a bit more”, and it is true, but life does not stop when you do. Sometimes clarity comes only after the step, not before it.

18-13-13.heading: Walking through doors into the unknown
paragraphs: You often close doors in your life before you can see the next ones. The Moon in your actions is the path between two towers that leads off into the unknown: you act while it is still dark ahead. Death appears in both energy and emotions. In the first role it gives strength through endings: you come alive once a worn-out form is let go and the space is cleared. In the second it means that you live through change in earnest: after an important ending you change too, not just your circumstances.

**You know how to go through transitions where the old has ended and the new cannot yet be seen.** Leaving a job with no plan lined up, a move, the end of a long habit — you do not pretend nothing has happened, but you do not stand on the threshold for years either. Once you have grieved, you step into the unclear and make a home there. Others are often surprised that you dare. For you, though, living in what is worn out is harder than going into the unfamiliar.

It is harder when imagination runs ahead of events. The Moon paints a loss where so far there is only a difficult stretch: a relationship is going through a crisis, work has stalled — and inwardly you are already saying goodbye. Your feelings travel the whole road of an ending, and the strength that comes from endings pushes you to put a full stop. That way you can end something where an honest conversation would have been enough. Before letting go, it is worth checking whether this really is the end.

18-14-5.heading: Leaning on routine in uncertain times
paragraphs: In uncertain times simple things hold you steady: Sunday dinner with the family, tried-and-tested rules, advice from someone you trust. The Hierophant in emotions explains this need: you feel at peace where there are shared values, tradition, a clear “this is how we do things”. The Moon shows why it matters so much: you often have to act in poor light, when much is unknown. Temperance shares out your strength: little by little you blend work and rest, the new and the familiar, without rushing to extremes.

When everything is changing at work and plans are hazy, you do not rush about: you keep to your routine, turn to the experience of people who have been there longer, keep up familiar rituals. The unknown does not disappear because of this, but it stops filling all the space. An island of stability forms around you, and others lean on it too. **Uncertainty is easier to bear when there is a way of life you can come back to.**

A rule can also become a shield against the unknown. Someone close to you makes an unusual choice — changes profession, lives differently from what is expected. The Moon instantly paints worrying scenarios, and instead of asking “how do you see it?” you say “that’s not how things are done”. You want to protect them, but they hear judgement. The way of life that was meant to bring peace begins to separate you from those who have chosen their own road.

18-15-6.heading: An attraction you want to choose yourself
paragraphs: You are drawn to people and pursuits strongly — so strongly that both you and those around you notice. The Devil in energy speaks of the source of your strength: it comes from attraction, from the wish to be closer to whatever beckons. But this card also has a chain: a strong pull can bind. The Lovers shape your response: you live through everything important via your bond with another person and via the choice of whom to be with. The Moon in your actions adds imagination: where not everything is clear, you act on a picture you have filled in yourself.

**Attraction gives you strength, and choice makes it yours.** When you are taken with a person or a shared cause, you have energy for a great deal: you look for chances to meet, think up ways to help, are ready for a long road. It works best when you consciously tell yourself “yes, I choose this” — and know you could choose otherwise. Then the pull does not hold you, it leads you.

The weak spot is imagination: it ties you to an image rather than to the person. When things are unclear, you fill in what the other person feels and wants, and hold on to that picture. A late reply turns into a whole story, an evasive phrase into a reason for anxiety. The more guesses, the tighter the grip, and the real person drifts further and further from the one you have drawn for yourself. Asking directly seems dangerous: what if the picture collapses?

18-15-15.heading: Strong desires in a deceptive light
paragraphs: Some things pull at you harder than you can explain, and the overall tone of your life grows out of that depth. The Moon sets the rhythm of what you do: you take things on when only part of the road is visible, and you go by impression rather than by map. The Devil holds two places. In how your strength is spread, he is a source: for the sake of what truly draws you, you can make an effort you never expected of yourself. In what you live through, he gives you a grip — you want a lucky streak to last, and it is hard to part with what has become yours.

**Your strength comes through when a desire steps out of the shadows and gets a name.** Say a new pastime has drawn you in: evening after evening you come back to it, though nobody asks you to. While the reason stays in the half-light, it simply eats up your time. But once you look calmly at what exactly draws you — the thrill, recognition, money, a sense of mastery over your material — you have a choice: how much to give it and what to expect in return. Then the depth of your desire works for you instead of leading you round in circles.

It gets harder when, in that uncertain light, desire and fear become impossible to tell apart. A job, a relationship or a familiar way of life may have stopped bringing you joy long ago, yet your imagination at once paints how empty things would be without it. So you hold on — no longer because you want to, but because letting go feels like losing a part of yourself. Your strength goes into keeping things as they are. The chain is held not by the desire itself but by a picture of the future that nobody has ever checked.

18-16-7.heading: Setting a course through the fog
captions: The joy of a milestone reached
paragraphs: Much in your life gets going before it becomes clear. The Moon sets the rhythm of what you do: you take the first step when only part of the way can be seen, and fill in the rest with guesswork. The Chariot shapes your response: you feel most alive when you are steering events yourself and can see you are making headway, while any setback feels like a defeat. The Tower shows how your strength is spread: for long stretches it builds up in a single structure — a plan, an agreement, an idea of how things work. If its foundation turns out to be false, everything you put in is lost at once, along with it.

**You can move decisively where others wait for everything to be clear.** Say you take on a move or a new venture where half the conditions are unknown. You set a goal, get going and work out the rest along the way. This holds as long as the map stays a sketch for you: every few steps you check it against what has come into view and adjust the route. The direction is still yours; the plan simply changes with the terrain instead of waiting for reality to run into it.

The risk is that the Chariot finds it hard to admit a wrong turn: it feels like losing. Then a guess turns into a fortress. Your imagination fills the gaps, warning signs look like just another obstacle to overcome, and more and more of your strength goes into defending the plan. When the foundation gives way, everything that stood on it falls at once: time, money, promises made to people. On top of the loss itself comes the bitterness of personal defeat, although all that was wrong was the guess everything rested on.

18-16-16.heading: Building on shifting ground
paragraphs: It matters to you to know what everything rests on. The Moon sets the rhythm of what you do: you move in the half-light and fill in what is missing with guesswork, because you almost never have the full picture before taking a step. The Tower plays two roles here. In how your strength is spread, it makes the outflow uneven: for long stretches your effort goes into building something — a plan, an agreement, a way of life — and if the foundation gives way, it all goes at once into getting through the fall and clearing the rubble. In what you live through, it marks the moment when an old explanation turns out to be wrong: you feel this not as a correction but as a collapse.

**The strength of this combination is telling what you know from what you only guess.** Before a big step — a move, a shared venture, a major purchase — you ask not only “do I like this?” but also “what does it stand on?” What has been checked, and what only seems so for now? You leave a guess as a guess and do not put your whole weight on it. What you build may look more modest than other people’s castles, but you know which wall is load-bearing.

The other side is living in expectation of a blow. If any structure might fall, it is easier not to build anything in earnest: not to settle into a new place, not to commit fully to a venture, to keep the people close to you at a distance “just in case”. Good news is met with the question of where the catch is. Your imagination draws cracks where there are none, and your strength goes into bracing for a disaster that never comes. There is no collapse, but nothing to lean on either: life turns into a temporary camp.
